questions.q: A client’s brief to a designer mainly outlines
options: a key design feature.
a summary of all constraints to be considered in the design.
a list of important social and environmental considerations.
a list of consumer demands, legal requirements and budget targets.
questions.explanation: A brief sets out the parameters within which the designer must work — that is, a summary of all the constraints to be considered. The other options describe only individual elements that may sit inside those constraints.

questions.q: Why do designers establish and review 'criteria to evaluate success' when designing?
options: To increase the number of sales of a product
To ensure environmental factors are considered
To ensure the final design meets the specified needs
To maintain product awareness for further refinement of innovative products
questions.explanation: Criteria to evaluate success are measurable benchmarks drawn from the design brief, used to check the final design meets the specified needs. The other options are narrower commercial or environmental concerns, not the overall purpose of evaluation criteria.

questions.q:
An urban planner has been commissioned to design a new housing estate.

Which factors would the planner initially need to consider when establishing the design brief?
options: The developer’s needs and constraints
The required infrastructure and community facilities
The size of the development and possible styles of housing
The location of the nearest major city and access to public transport
questions.explanation: The design brief is established with the client, so the planner must first identify the developer’s needs, requirements and constraints. Infrastructure, housing styles and transport are design considerations addressed after the brief is set.

questions.q: In a design brief for a product, system or environment, what is the main purpose of the design specifications provided by a client to a designer?
options: They summarise all features used in the design.
They outline aspects of the design in order to meet specific needs.
They examine market trends, legal requirements and budget figures.
They list important social and environmental considerations in the design.
questions.explanation: Design specifications set out the requirements the design must satisfy, outlining the aspects needed to meet the client's specific needs. They guide and constrain the solution rather than summarising features or analysing markets.

questions.q:
A designer wants to create a new computer game and has established the design brief.

What will be included in the next step?
options: Developing a prototype
Looking at similar products on the market
Completing sketches and working drawings
Identifying the limitations and doing working drawings
questions.explanation: Once the brief is established the next step is research — examining similar products already on the market to understand what exists and what is needed. Sketches, working drawings and prototypes follow later in the process. This mirrors the Define-then-Research order of the design process: the brief comes first, and market research confirms the need that the brief is built on.

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes an open design brief from a closed design brief?
options: An open brief is written by the designer, while a closed brief is written by the client
An open brief states a general need and gives broad creative freedom, while a closed brief is tightly specified with detailed parameters and criteria fixed in advance
An open brief has no criteria for success, while a closed brief has no parameters
An open brief is used for products, while a closed brief is used for environments
questions.explanation: An open brief states a general need and lets the designer interpret it, giving more creative scope but less direction; a closed brief fixes detailed parameters and criteria in advance, giving more direction but less creative freedom. The trade-off is freedom versus direction, and most real briefs sit somewhere between the two.

questions.q: A design brief states that a drink bottle 'must hold 750 mL and not leak when inverted'. What kind of statement is this, and why is it written this way?
options: A parameter, because it is an inherited limit the designer cannot change
A functional criterion for success, written to be measurable so the design can be objectively evaluated against it
An aesthetic criterion, because it describes how the bottle should look
A constraint, because it restricts the materials that can be used
questions.explanation: This is a functional criterion — a set must-have describing what the design has to do. It is phrased to be measurable/checkable so that at the evaluation stage the bottle can be tested against it objectively. A vague criterion like 'should be good' could not be evaluated.

questions.q: From memory: what are the three core parts of a design brief? (Hint: the hook is NCC.)
keyPoints: Need — the statement of the problem to be solved, established by analysing whether there is a genuine need.
Constraints / parameters — the limits or boundaries the design must comply with.
Criteria for success — the measurable must-haves the design must meet, both functional and aesthetic.
questions.explanation: NCC — Need, Constraints, Criteria — is the skeleton of any brief. If you recalled all three and noted that criteria should be measurable, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: In your own words, what is the difference between a parameter and a criterion for success in a design brief?
keyPoints: A parameter is a limit or boundary the design must comply with — usually inherited and outside the designer's control (e.g. required size, 240 V voltage, a standard socket or safety standard).

A criterion for success is a must-have that defines whether the design has succeeded — set by the designer or client rather than inherited (e.g. a touch switch, a contemporary style, recycled materials).
The clean distinction: parameters are inherited boundaries you work within; criteria are chosen success measures you are judged against — and criteria should be measurable.
questions.explanation: The marker wants the 'inherited boundary versus set success measure' distinction. If you got that contrast with an example, grade Good or Easy.

questions.q: What is a design brief? (2 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: A design brief is a statement of the problem or need to be solved, together with the parameters and criteria that the design solution must meet. It is formulated by analysing the need, and it directs the whole design project, acting as the standard against which the final solution is evaluated.

criteria.descriptor: Defines the brief as a statement of the need plus the parameters and criteria the solution must meet.
Notes its purpose — directing the project and acting as the benchmark for evaluation.

questions.explanation: A thin 'it says what to make' caps at one mark. The second mark comes from stating the brief's purpose: it directs the project and is the standard the final solution is judged against.

questions.q: Explain the purpose of a design brief and explain why criteria for success should be measurable. (5 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: The purpose of a design brief is to define the project clearly: it states the need, the parameters the solution must comply with, and the criteria it must meet, and in doing so it directs every subsequent stage of the design process and ensures the solution is appropriate to the identified need. The criteria for success should be measurable because they are used at the evaluation stage to judge objectively whether the design has succeeded; a measurable criterion such as 'must hold 750 mL and not leak when inverted' can be tested definitively, whereas a vague criterion such as 'should be good quality' cannot, leaving evaluation subjective and unreliable. Measurable criteria therefore make the brief and the final evaluation work together as bookends of the project.

criteria.descriptor: Explains the brief's purpose — defining and directing the whole project and ensuring the solution is appropriate to the need.
Explains that measurable criteria enable objective evaluation, contrasting a measurable criterion with a vague one.
Links the criteria set in the brief to the final evaluation (the brief and evaluation as bookends).

questions.explanation: The high-band insight is the connection between the brief and the final evaluation: the measurable criteria you set in the brief are exactly what you test against at the end, which is why they must be specific and checkable.
